elements.element: Customer is not subject to any restriction on soliciting the other party’s employees or personnel.
elements.evidence: The rendered clause expressly binds “both parties,” including Customer, not to solicit specified employees for employment.
The restriction applies to “both parties” and covers employees of the other party.

elements.element: The restriction applies only to personnel directly involved in the services.
elements.evidence: It is limited to employees “directly involved in the provision or receipt of services under this Agreement.”

elements.element: The restriction lasts for 12 months from the end of each covered person’s involvement in the services.
elements.evidence: The clause instead applies during the Agreement and for one year after the Agreement ends. It is not triggered by the end of each person’s involvement and may therefore last longer than 12 months after that involvement ends.

elements.element: General advertisements and recruitment campaigns not specifically targeted at covered personnel are excluded.
elements.evidence: The proviso excludes “general advertisements or recruitment campaigns not specifically targeted at such employees.”

elements.element: Unsolicited approaches by covered personnel are excluded.
elements.evidence: The proviso states that hiring a person who “approaches a party on an unsolicited basis” does not breach the restriction.

elements.element: The clause restricts solicitation only and does not prohibit hiring as such.
elements.evidence: The operative prohibition is limited to soliciting for employment; it does not independently prohibit hiring. The proviso also expressly permits hiring advertisement respondents and unsolicited applicants.

result.reason: The redline successfully converts the no-hire into a mutual, service-personnel-specific non-solicit and includes both required carve-outs. However, it retains an agreement-based duration rather than imposing 12 months measured from the end of each individual’s involvement, so the fallback is not fully satisfied. The proviso is understandable but has awkward “neither ... or ... nor” construction.
